tucker.title: Programming Languages: Principles and Paradigms
tucker.authors: Allen B. Tucker and Robert E. Noonan

programming-fundamentals-and-language-ty.read: Chapter 2: Evolution of the Major Programming Languages
programming-fundamentals-and-language-ty.why: The history of FORTRAN, ALGOL, LISP, COBOL, BASIC, Pascal, C, C++ and Java that the course book surveys.

programming-paradigms.read: Chapter 1 (paradigms) and Chapters 12–14: Imperative, Object-Oriented and Functional Programming
programming-paradigms.why: The course book cites Tucker and Noonan (2002); these chapters cover the same paradigms.

evaluating-programming-languages.why: Readability, writability and reliability, the three main criteria the 2024/25 paper asks for.

syntax-bnf-and-ambiguity.why: BNF, EBNF, syntax diagrams, parse trees and ambiguity.
The grammars, lexical syntax and dangling-else example the course book uses.

type-systems-overloading-and-casting.why: Types, type maps, static and dynamic typing, conversions — the source of the course book's examples.

control-structures-scope-and-binding.read: Chapter 5: Names, Bindings, and Scopes; Chapter 8: Statement-Level Control Structures
control-structures-scope-and-binding.why: Binding times, lifetime, scope, aliasing and loop and selection statements.

memory-management-in-programs.why: Stack frames, parameter passing and the static area, stack and heap as the course book describes them.
